description: Triggering accuracy and domain correctness tests for finance skills

evals.prompt: My client wants to roll their 401k into an IRA with us. We're a dual-registrant — I handle some accounts as a broker and some as an adviser. Which standard of care applies to this rollover recommendation, and what documentation do I need to keep? The account is about $340K and they're 58 years old.
evals.expected_output: Should identify this as a Reg BI recommendation (rollover from ERISA plan to IRA via broker-dealer capacity), cite the four Reg BI obligations (Disclosure, Care, Conflict of Interest, Compliance), mention PTE 2020-02 for the ERISA side, and discuss documentation of reasonably available alternatives. Should NOT default to fiduciary analysis unless the adviser capacity is explicitly chosen.

assertions.text: Mentions Reg BI by name
Cites the four Reg BI obligations
Mentions PTE 2020-02 or DOL prohibited transaction exemption
Discusses reasonably available alternatives analysis
Does not incorrectly apply pure fiduciary standard without acknowledging BD capacity

evals.prompt: We're an RIA and one of our advisers just recommended a proprietary fund to a client when a cheaper third-party option with similar performance exists. The client is a retired teacher, moderate risk tolerance, $600K portfolio. Is there a fiduciary issue here?
evals.expected_output: Should apply IA Act Section 206 fiduciary analysis — duty of care (was the recommendation in the client's best interest given cheaper alternative?) and duty of loyalty (proprietary fund creates a conflict). Should discuss whether the conflict was disclosed, mitigated, and whether the adviser can demonstrate the recommendation was still in the client's best interest despite the cost differential.

assertions.text: Applies IA Act Section 206 fiduciary framework
Analyzes both duty of care and duty of loyalty
Identifies proprietary fund as conflict of interest
Discusses cost differential materiality
Does not apply FINRA suitability as primary standard

evals.prompt: I'm building out the fee schedule section of our Form ADV Part 2A. We charge a tiered AUM fee (1.0% on first $1M, 0.75% on next $2M, 0.50% above $3M), plus a $2,500 annual financial planning fee. We also get 12b-1 fees from some mutual fund positions. How should we disclose all of this?
evals.expected_output: Should focus on disclosure requirements — Form ADV Item 5 structure, how to present the tiered AUM schedule, requirement to disclose the financial planning fee as a separate service, obligation to disclose 12b-1 fees as indirect compensation creating a conflict, and reference to Reg BI CRS fee disclosure if applicable. Should NOT focus on billing mechanics (how to calculate, prorate, or collect fees).

assertions.text: References Form ADV Part 2A Item 5
Addresses 12b-1 fee disclosure as indirect compensation or conflict
Discusses how to present tiered fee schedules in disclosure documents
Provides 3+ specific rule numbers or regulatory citations
Identifies 3+ distinct edge cases or pitfalls in fee disclosure
Focuses on regulatory disclosure requirements, not billing system implementation

evals.prompt: I need to set up our quarterly billing process. We bill in advance on AUM as of the last business day of the prior quarter, with new accounts prorated from their funding date. When a client terminates mid-quarter we refund the unused portion. How should I structure the billing calculation and what edge cases do I need to handle?
evals.expected_output: Should focus on billing mechanics — AUM valuation date selection, proration formulas for new/terminated accounts, mid-quarter termination refund calculation, handling of account additions/withdrawals during the quarter, billing frequency, custodian fee deduction setup, and reconciliation. Should NOT primarily discuss disclosure obligations.

assertions.text: Provides proration formula or methodology for partial-quarter accounts
Addresses mid-quarter termination refund calculation
Discusses billing system mechanics (custodian deduction, valuation dates)
Identifies 4+ distinct edge cases or pitfalls in billing
Outlines 5+ steps or phases in the billing process
Focuses on operational billing implementation, not regulatory disclosure

evals.prompt: We're onboarding a new institutional client — a family trust with three trustees, two of whom are US persons and one is a UK resident. The trust document names a corporate trustee as well. Walk me through the compliance requirements for opening this account.
evals.expected_output: Should focus on CIP/KYC verification for all trustees (including the foreign person), beneficial ownership certification for the entity, OFAC screening of all parties, risk-based approval tier (elevated due to foreign trustee), enhanced due diligence triggers, and documentation requirements. Should NOT focus on operational workflow steps like NIGO management or custodian submission mechanics.

assertions.text: Addresses CIP/KYC for each trustee individually
Mentions beneficial ownership certification requirement
Flags the non-US trustee as requiring enhanced due diligence
References OFAC or sanctions screening
Provides 3+ specific rule numbers or regulatory citations
Identifies 3+ distinct edge cases or pitfalls specific to trust entities with foreign persons

evals.prompt: Our NIGO rate for new accounts submitted to Schwab is running at 28%. Most rejections are missing signatures, incorrect entity titling, and incomplete beneficiary designations. I need to redesign our account opening workflow to get this under 10%. What should the new process look like?
evals.expected_output: Should focus on operational workflow redesign — document validation gates, pre-submission QC checks, digital signature integration, common titling error patterns and how to prevent them, NIGO root cause analysis, STP rate improvement tactics, and custodian submission best practices.

assertions.text: Addresses NIGO root cause analysis and specific rejection patterns
Proposes workflow validation gates or pre-submission checks
Discusses operational process improvement (not just compliance requirements)
Mentions specific custodian integration or submission mechanics
Outlines 5+ steps or phases in the redesigned workflow
Identifies 4+ distinct edge cases or pitfalls in account opening

evals.prompt: I'm looking at a fund that returned 12% annualized over the last 5 years with a standard deviation of 18%. The max drawdown was -32% during COVID. How do I assess whether the risk-adjusted returns are actually good, and what metrics should I use to compare it against its benchmark?
evals.expected_output: Should analyze realized/historical risk metrics — Sharpe ratio calculation from the given data, Sortino ratio, maximum drawdown analysis, recovery time, comparison to benchmark using tracking error and information ratio. Should ground analysis in the historical data provided, not project future scenarios.

assertions.text: Calculates or discusses Sharpe ratio using provided return and volatility data
Analyzes the -32% max drawdown in context (severity, recovery)
Mentions Sortino ratio or downside risk metrics
Provides 3+ specific risk metrics with explanations
Analysis is grounded in historical/realized data, not forward projections

evals.prompt: I'm building a new portfolio for a client with a 15-year horizon. I need to estimate the probability that a 70/30 stock/bond allocation will fail to meet their 6% real return target. What risk models and simulation approaches should I use?
evals.expected_output: Should discuss forward-looking risk modeling — Monte Carlo simulation, capital market assumptions (expected returns, volatilities, correlations), scenario analysis, regime-switching models, fat-tail adjustments. Should focus on projecting future outcomes, not analyzing past performance.

assertions.text: Discusses Monte Carlo simulation or stochastic modeling
Mentions capital market assumptions or expected return estimation
Addresses probability of meeting the return target over the time horizon
Focus is on forward projection methodology, not historical analysis

evals.prompt: Our account transfer process currently requires manual intervention for about 60% of incoming ACATs. The ops team is copying data between three systems and manually matching transfer items against our records. I want to automate this to get our STP rate above 90%. What approach should I take?
evals.expected_output: Should focus on straight-through processing methodology — measuring current STP rate, identifying manual touchpoints, exception-based processing design, API vs RPA evaluation for the three-system integration, exception categorization and auto-resolution rules, and STP benchmarking targets for transfer processing.

assertions.text: Defines or calculates STP rate and sets improvement targets
Identifies exception categories and auto-resolution patterns
Discusses API vs RPA integration approaches for legacy systems
Outlines 5+ steps or phases in the automation approach
Identifies 3+ distinct edge cases or pitfalls in transfer automation
Focus is on end-to-end automation and exception handling, not task routing or approvals

evals.prompt: I need to build an approval workflow for account maintenance requests. Address changes need one approval, beneficiary changes need two approvals with a compliance review, and re-registrations need three approvals including a supervisor sign-off. Each level has different SLA targets and escalation rules. How should I design this?
evals.expected_output: Should focus on workflow design — multi-level approval chains, delegation of authority, SLA monitoring and escalation rules, task routing logic, state machine modeling for the different request types, and audit trail requirements.

assertions.text: Designs multi-level approval chain with different thresholds by request type
Addresses SLA targets and escalation rules for aging items
Discusses task routing or state machine modeling
Outlines 5+ steps or phases in the workflow design
Focus is on approval chains and routing, not end-to-end STP rate optimization

evals.prompt: A client invested $100,000 in a fund. After 6 months the fund was up 15% and they added another $50,000. After another 6 months the total value is $178,000. Calculate both the time-weighted return (TWR) and the money-weighted return (MWR/IRR) and explain why they differ.
evals.expected_output: TWR: Sub-period 1 return = 15%. Sub-period 2: start value = $115K + $50K = $165K, end = $178K, return = 7.88%. TWR = (1.15)(1.0788) - 1 = 24.06%. MWR/IRR: solve -100K at t=0, -50K at t=0.5, +178K at t=1. IRR will be lower than TWR because more capital was deployed after the stronger period. Should clearly explain the divergence.

assertions.text: TWR calculation is approximately 24% (range 23.5-24.5%)
MWR/IRR is lower than TWR
Shows sub-period return calculations step by step
Identifies TWR as manager skill, MWR as investor experience

evals.prompt: We're a broker-dealer and one of our reps has a turnover ratio of 8.2 and a cost-to-equity ratio of 14% in a retired client's account. The client is 72 years old with moderate risk tolerance and a $420K account. The rep says the client approved every trade. What are the compliance issues?
evals.expected_output: Should identify quantitative suitability (FINRA Rule 2111 third prong) violations — turnover ratio above 6 is presumptively excessive, cost-to-equity ratio of 14% means the account must earn 14% just to break even. Client approval does not excuse excessive trading. Should flag churning indicators, senior investor protections, and recommended supervisory response.

assertions.text: Cites FINRA Rule 2111 quantitative suitability prong
Identifies turnover ratio above 6 as presumptively excessive
Explains cost-to-equity ratio meaning (account must earn 14% to break even)
States that client approval of individual trades does not cure excessive trading
Mentions senior investor protections given client age

evals.prompt: I have a taxable portfolio worth $800K that has drifted from its 60/40 target to 68/32 stocks/bonds. My threshold band is +/- 5%. I also have about $15K in unrealized losses in some equity positions. Should I rebalance, and if so, how should I coordinate with tax-loss harvesting?
evals.expected_output: Should identify that equities have breached the 5% band (68% vs 65% upper limit). Recommend selling ~$64K in equities to buy bonds. Should coordinate with TLH — harvest the $15K in losses first by selling losing positions as part of the rebalance sell, replace with similar (not substantially identical) securities to maintain exposure, and be aware of wash-sale rules (30-day window, across all accounts including retirement). Net effect: rebalance AND capture tax alpha.

assertions.text: Identifies that the 5% band has been breached (68% > 65%)
Calculates approximate rebalance trade size (~$64K)
Recommends harvesting the $15K loss as part of the rebalance
Warns about wash-sale rules
Mentions replacement security selection

evals.prompt: I'm preparing for a quarterly review meeting with a retired couple (ages 68 and 65). They have a $1.8M portfolio across IRA, Roth IRA, and taxable accounts. The husband turns 73 next year and will need to start RMDs. What should my review prep cover?
evals.expected_output: Should cover: performance vs benchmark and IPS targets, asset allocation drift check, RMD estimation for the husband's IRA (using Uniform Lifetime Table), tax-efficient withdrawal sequencing across the three account types, Roth conversion opportunity analysis before RMDs begin, income projection for the coming year, insurance review, and estate planning coordination.

assertions.text: Addresses RMD calculation and timing (husband turning 73)
Discusses tax-efficient withdrawal sequencing across IRA/Roth/taxable
Mentions Roth conversion opportunity before RMDs begin
Includes performance review against IPS or benchmark

evals.prompt: Walk me through what happens to a market order to buy 5,000 shares of AAPL from the moment I hit submit to when the shares appear in my account. Cover routing, execution, clearing, and settlement.
evals.expected_output: Should cover the full lifecycle: order entry and validation, smart order routing (consideration of exchanges, dark pools, Reg NMS Rule 611 order protection), execution venue selection, trade execution and fill confirmation, post-trade allocation, NSCC trade comparison and netting (CNS system), DTC settlement on T+1, and final position update in the client's account.

assertions.text: Mentions smart order routing and venue selection considerations
References Reg NMS or order protection rule
Describes NSCC clearing and netting process
States T+1 settlement cycle for US equities

evals.prompt: A client wants to transfer their $2.1M account from another broker-dealer to us via ACAT. The account has stocks, bonds, mutual funds, and some options positions. The sending firm is being slow — it's been 5 business days and we haven't received the assets. What are our options?
evals.expected_output: Should explain ACAT process and FINRA Rule 11870 timeline (3 business days to validate, then deliver within timeline). After 5 days, the sending firm may be in violation. Options: file a FINRA complaint, escalate via NSCC reclaim process. Should note that options may need special handling (not all options transfer via ACAT), mutual fund positions may need to be liquidated if not on the receiving firm's platform, and the client should be advised about potential costs.

assertions.text: References FINRA Rule 11870 and the ACAT timeline requirements
Identifies recourse options (FINRA complaint, NSCC escalation)
Notes that some assets may not transfer cleanly (options, proprietary funds)
Mentions the 3-business-day validation requirement

evals.prompt: I'm 64 and retiring in March with $1.4M saved. I keep reading about sequence of returns risk - if the market drops 20% in my first year, am I sunk? I was planning to take about $60K a year. Should I use guardrails instead of just fixed inflation-adjusted withdrawals?
evals.expected_output: Should explain sequence-of-returns risk (early losses plus withdrawals do permanent damage), compare fixed inflation-adjusted withdrawals to a Guyton-Klinger-style guardrails rule with upper/lower withdrawal-rate bands and 10% spending adjustments, and discuss mitigants like a cash buffer and flexible spending. Should NOT pivot to accumulation-side savings-rate math.

assertions.text: Mentions sequence of returns risk
Discusses guardrails with upper and lower withdrawal rate bands
Mentions the 4% rule and its fixed inflation-adjusted spending assumption
Discusses a spending cut at the upper guardrail
Does not pivot to accumulation savings rate math for hitting a retirement number

evals.prompt: I'm 41, making $145K, with $210K in my 401(k). I put in 10% of salary and get a 4% employer match. Am I on track to retire at 65, and how much should I be saving each month to get there?
evals.expected_output: Should project the accumulation path, estimate the retirement nest egg target, compute the required monthly savings rate to close any gap, credit the employer match, and mention catch-up contributions at 50. Should NOT center the answer on decumulation withdrawal mechanics like guardrails or RMDs.

assertions.text: Discusses the required monthly savings rate to stay on track
Mentions the employer match
Mentions a retirement savings target amount
Mentions catch-up contributions after age 50
Does not center the answer on safe withdrawal mechanics or RMD rules in retirement

evals.prompt: My mother is 82 with about a $6M estate. She wants to give me her taxable brokerage account now - it's worth $900K with maybe $200K of cost basis. Would it be smarter for her to gift it now or leave it to me in her will? And does the new $15 million exemption change anything?
evals.expected_output: Should frame this as the gift-now-vs-bequeath basis tradeoff: gifted assets carry over the donor's basis while bequeathed assets get a step-up at death, and with a $6M estate far under the $15M exemption (as of 2026) there is no estate tax benefit to offset losing the step-up. Should mention annual exclusion gifting of cash or high-basis assets as the alternative.

assertions.text: Mentions the step-up in basis at death
Mentions carryover basis for gifted assets
Mentions the $15 million lifetime exemption
Mentions the annual gift exclusion
Does not reduce the question to income-tax lot selection or asset location mechanics

evals.prompt: I'm 72, in the 24% bracket, and I give about $20K a year to my church out of my checking account. I have a $1.1M traditional IRA and a taxable account full of appreciated index funds. Is there a smarter way to do this giving from a tax standpoint - QCDs, donating shares, bunching into a donor-advised fund?
evals.expected_output: Should focus on the income-tax mechanics of charitable giving: qualified charitable distributions from the IRA (client is over 70 1/2), donating appreciated securities to avoid capital gains, and bunching deductions through a donor-advised fund relative to the standard deduction. Should NOT drift into estate exemption, portability, or Form 706 planning.

assertions.text: Mentions a qualified charitable distribution
Mentions donor-advised fund bunching
Mentions giving appreciated shares to avoid capital gains
Mentions the standard deduction
Does not drift into estate exemption portability or Form 706 planning

evals.prompt: I just had 3,000 RSUs vest at $92 and I also hold 2,000 ISOs with a $12 strike while the 409A price is $45. My employer only withheld 22% on the RSU income and I'm definitely in the 35% bracket. Am I going to owe AMT if I exercise the ISOs and hold this year?
evals.expected_output: Should identify the RSU supplemental-withholding gap (22% flat rate vs 35% marginal rate means a balance due at filing) and treat the ISO exercise-and-hold as an AMT preference item on the spread, walking through the AMT exposure and the minimum tax credit. Should NOT answer with generic asset location or Roth conversion advice.

assertions.text: Mentions the supplemental withholding rate on RSU income
Mentions the ISO spread as an AMT preference item
Mentions the alternative minimum tax
Mentions the AMT credit in future years
Does not answer with generic asset location or Roth conversion sequencing advice

evals.prompt: I have $500K in a taxable brokerage, $700K in a traditional 401(k), and $150K in a Roth IRA. Which accounts should hold my bond funds versus my stock index funds? And does it ever make sense to do Roth conversions in my early retirement years before Social Security starts?
evals.expected_output: Should give asset-location guidance (tax-inefficient bonds in the tax-deferred 401(k), tax-efficient equity index funds in taxable, highest-growth assets in Roth) and discuss partial Roth conversions filling low brackets in the gap years before Social Security and RMDs. Should NOT treat this as an equity-compensation or AMT question.

assertions.text: Discusses asset location across taxable and tax-deferred accounts
Mentions bonds in the tax-deferred account
Discusses a Roth conversion in low bracket years
Mentions the gap years before Social Security begins
Does not treat this as an equity compensation or AMT exercise timing question

evals.prompt: I ran my fund's monthly excess returns against the Fama-French factors: alpha 0.03 per month with a t-stat of 0.5, market beta 0.99, HML loading 0.45 with a t-stat of 23, R-squared 0.986. The fund charges 0.85%. Is this manager actually adding skill or am I just paying active fees for a value tilt?
evals.expected_output: Should interpret the regression: the alpha is statistically insignificant (t well below 2) while the HML loading is a strong, significant value tilt, so the fund's returns are factor exposure, not skill, and could be replicated with a cheap value-tilted index fund - making it a fee question. Should NOT answer purely with Sharpe or capture ratio comparisons.

assertions.text: Mentions the alpha is not statistically significant
Identifies the value factor loading as the return driver
Mentions manager skill and factor exposure
Mentions a cheaper index or factor fund replication
Does not answer purely with Sharpe ratio or capture ratio comparisons

evals.prompt: Two balanced funds: Fund A returned 9.1% annualized with 11% volatility, Fund B returned 10.4% with 16% volatility. The risk-free rate is 4%. Fund B also has worse downside capture. Which one actually performed better after adjusting for risk, and which ratios should I use to compare them?
evals.expected_output: Should compute Sharpe ratios from the given data (A: 5.1/11 = 0.46, B: 6.4/16 = 0.40), bring in Sortino and downside capture for downside risk, and conclude A wins per unit of risk. Should NOT recast the question as a factor regression.

assertions.text: Calculates the Sharpe ratio for each fund
Mentions the Sortino ratio for downside risk
Discusses downside capture
Mentions risk-adjusted return per unit of risk
Does not recast the question as a Fama-French factor regression

evals.prompt: I'm reading a company's 10-K. Net income was $60M but cash from operations was $75M, capex was $35M, and receivables jumped 40% on only 12% revenue growth. How do I get from these statements to free cash flow, and should I be worried about the quality of the earnings?
evals.expected_output: Should build FCFF/FCFE from CFO and capex, explain the FCFF vs FCFE distinction, compute or discuss the accruals ratio, and flag receivables growing far faster than revenue as a revenue-recognition red flag. Should NOT jump to a DCF intrinsic-value estimate.

assertions.text: Calculates free cash flow from operating cash flow and capex
Mentions the accruals ratio earnings quality signal
Flags receivables growing faster than revenue
Mentions FCFF or FCFE free cash flow measures
Does not jump to a DCF terminal value or intrinsic value estimate

evals.prompt: I want to value this stock with a DCF. Free cash flow is $47.5M, I expect 8% growth for five years and then 2.5% terminal growth, and WACC is around 9%. Walk me through getting to a fair value per share, and where can the terminal value assumptions go wrong?
evals.expected_output: Should project and discount the cash flows at WACC, compute a Gordon-growth terminal value, bridge enterprise value to equity value per share, and stress the sensitivity of fair value to the terminal growth and discount rate spread. Should NOT spend the answer re-deriving FCFF from the statements.

assertions.text: Mentions the terminal value in the DCF
Mentions the WACC discount rate
Calculates enterprise value and value per share
Mentions sensitivity of fair value to terminal growth assumptions
Does not spend the answer on earnings quality or statement analysis instead of valuation

evals.prompt: A client wants to put $250K into a private real estate fund a friend of hers is raising under Reg D. She made $210K last year and $185K the year before, and her net worth is about $850K not counting her house. The sponsor has been advertising the deal on Instagram. Can she invest, and what do I need to check first?
evals.expected_output: Should run the Rule 501(a) accredited tests (income under $200K in one of the two most recent years, net worth under $1M ex-residence - she likely fails both), flag the Instagram posts as general solicitation forcing the offering into 506(c) with mandatory verification, and note the adviser must screen eligibility before any best-interest analysis. Should NOT treat this as a hedge fund strategy and fee evaluation.

assertions.text: Mentions the accredited investor income and net worth tests
Identifies the Instagram advertising as general solicitation
Mentions reasonable steps to verify accredited status
Mentions net worth excluding the primary residence
Does not treat this as a hedge fund strategy and fee evaluation

evals.prompt: My client is looking at a long/short equity hedge fund charging 2-and-20 with an 8% hurdle and a one-year lockup. How do I evaluate whether the strategy and the fee structure are worth it versus just holding index funds? And if we also add a private equity fund, what should I know about the J-curve?
evals.expected_output: Should evaluate the hedge fund on investment merits: the 2-and-20 fee load against the hurdle, carried interest mechanics, lockup and liquidity terms, strategy fit, and the PE J-curve of early negative returns with IRR/TVPI-style performance measurement. Should NOT turn the answer into a Reg D eligibility analysis.

assertions.text: Explains the 2-and-20 fee structure and hurdle rate
Mentions the J-curve in private equity
Mentions carried interest
Discusses lockup and liquidity terms
Does not turn the answer into a Reg D accredited investor eligibility analysis

evals.prompt: I'm 66, retiring next year with $1.6M, and Social Security will cover about half of my $80K annual spending. I'm nervous about outliving my money. Does it make sense to put part of the portfolio into an immediate annuity as longevity insurance and build my income plan around that floor?
evals.expected_output: Should frame the SPIA as longevity insurance inside the income plan: mortality credits let it out-pay a self-insured portfolio, a floor-and-upside design annuitizes enough (with Social Security) to cover essential spending while the rest stays invested, reducing sequence and longevity risk on the withdrawal plan. Should NOT center on product features like surrender charges and rider fees.

assertions.text: Mentions the annuity as longevity insurance
Mentions mortality credits
Discusses a guaranteed income floor for essential expenses
Mentions sequence of returns risk or the withdrawal rate on the remaining portfolio
Does not center on product features like surrender charges, caps, and rider fees

evals.prompt: An agent is pitching my 58-year-old client a fixed indexed annuity with a 10% first-year surrender charge that declines over 9 years, a 5.5% cap on the index crediting, and an income rider that costs 1.1% a year. How do the surrender charges and the cap actually work, and is this product any good for her?
evals.expected_output: Should explain the product mechanics: the declining surrender charge schedule locking up liquidity, caps and participation rates limiting index credits (and being repriceable), the rider fee drag, and whether the annuity is suitable for this client versus simpler alternatives. Should NOT answer as retirement income plan design around guardrails and withdrawal rates.

assertions.text: Explains the surrender charge schedule
Discusses the participation rate and cap on index returns
Discusses the income rider cost
Discusses suitability of the annuity for this client
Does not answer as retirement income plan design around guardrails and safe withdrawal rates

evals.prompt: For a company with revenue of $500M, COGS $300M, SG&A $80M, D&A $30M, interest expense $10M, a 25% tax rate, a $15M increase in net working capital, capex of $35M, and net borrowing of $5M - calculate EBITDA, FCFF, and FCFE, and show your work.
evals.expected_output: EBIT = 500 - 300 - 80 - 30 = $90M; EBITDA = 90 + 30 = $120M; net income = (90 - 10) x 0.75 = $60M; CFO = 60 + 30 - 15 = $75M; FCFF = 75 + 10 x 0.75 - 35 = $47.5M (same from the EBIT route); FCFE = 75 - 35 + 5 = $45.0M. Should show both FCFF routes agreeing and note net income overstates distributable cash.

assertions.text: EBITDA is approximately $120M
FCFF is approximately $47.5M
FCFE is approximately $45M
Net income is approximately $60M
Mentions FCFF and FCFE

evals.prompt: My client exercised 5,000 ISOs at a $10 strike when the FMV was $50 and is holding the shares. Her other AMTI is $250,000 (married filing jointly) and her regular tax is $60,000. Using an AMT exemption of $137,000 and the 28% rate starting at $220,000 of AMT base, how much AMT will she owe on top of her regular tax, and is it money gone forever?
evals.expected_output: AMT preference = 5,000 x ($50 - $10) = $200,000; AMTI = $450,000; AMT base = $450,000 - $137,000 = $313,000; TMT = 26% x $220,000 + 28% x $93,000 = $57,200 + $26,040 = $83,240; AMT due = $83,240 - $60,000 = $23,240. Should explain the minimum tax credit carryforward and the higher $50 AMT basis in the shares.

assertions.text: AMT preference from the ISO spread is approximately $200K
Tentative minimum tax is approximately $83.2K
Incremental AMT due is approximately $23.2K
Mentions the AMT credit for future years
Mentions the higher AMT basis in the shares

evals.prompt: My client turns 73 this year. Her traditional IRA was worth $850,000 on December 31 of last year. What is her RMD for the year, and what is the penalty if she misses it entirely?
evals.expected_output: RMD = $850,000 / 26.5 (Uniform Lifetime Table divisor at age 73) = $32,075.47. Missed entirely: 25% excise tax on the shortfall = $8,018.87, reduced to 10% ($3,207.55) if corrected within the correction window under SECURE 2.0.

assertions.text: RMD is approximately $32.1K
Mentions the Uniform Lifetime Table divisor
The excise tax penalty if missed is approximately $8K
Mentions the reduced penalty if corrected within the correction window
Mentions the excise tax on the RMD shortfall

evals.prompt: A fund has monthly return volatility of 4.30%, an R-squared of 0.99 against its benchmark, and an 0.85% expense ratio; a comparable index fund charges 0.05%. Compute the annualized tracking error and the breakeven information ratio, and tell me whether this looks like a closet indexer.
evals.expected_output: Residual vol = 4.30% x sqrt(1 - 0.99) = 0.43% per month; tracking error = 0.43% x sqrt(12) = 1.49% annualized; fee gap = 0.80%; breakeven IR = 0.80 / 1.49 = 0.54. R-squared >= 0.98 and tracking error <= 2% both trip the closet-index screen; a 0.54 IR just to break even on fees is implausible, so hold the index fund instead.

assertions.text: Annualized tracking error is approximately 1.5%
Fee gap is approximately 0.8%
Calculates the breakeven information ratio
Identifies a closet index fund given high R-squared and low tracking error
Mentions monthly residual volatility

evals.prompt: Run a needs-based life insurance analysis for Spouse A: salary $110K (Spouse B earns $70K), mortgage $320K, other debts $25K, two kids who need $120K each for college, $60K per year of income replacement for 15 years discounted at a 3% real rate, and $15K of final expenses. Existing resources: $220K of group life on A and $150K of taxable investments earmarked for survivors. How much coverage should A buy?
evals.expected_output: Needs: $15K final + $345K debt + $240K education + PV of income replacement $60K x 11.938 = ~$716K, totaling ~$1,316,000. Less $370K of resources = ~$946K net need; recommend rounding up to a $1M 20-year level term policy, noting group coverage disappears at job change.

assertions.text: PV of income replacement is approximately $716K
Total capital needs are approximately $1.3M
Net coverage need is approximately $946K
Recommends a level term policy
Mentions the group life coverage and existing investments as offsets

evals.prompt: A widowed client with an $8M estate holds stock worth $1,000,000 with a $100,000 cost basis and wants her daughter to have it. Should she gift it now or leave it in her will?
